own_scenes.desc: Junto al funk, la otra gran lección rítmica del postpunk: el bajo como protagonista, el espacio y el eco de la producción dub. Las técnicas de estudio de Jamaica (King Tubby, Lee Perry) se convierten en herramienta de vanguardia para PiL, The Slits, The Pop Group y On-U Sound.

notes.chapter: Cap. 1: Mi imagen pública me pertenece: John Lydon y PiL
notes.text: En «The Punk and His Music» (Capital Radio, julio de 1977) Lydon pone roots reggae, Velvet, Can, Captain Beefheart y Peter Hammill, «una lista de temas para un movimiento postpunk que aún había de nacer». Para las bandas más aventureras el reggae es una revolución puramente sonora, «una psicodelia africanizada»: entre 1977 y 1981 su producción espacializada sienta la base de todo el postpunk experimental. Lydon viaja a Jamaica como consultor del sello Front Line de Virgin; con Don Letts frecuenta los «blues», fiestas reggae ilegales.

notes.chapter: Cap. 3: Resurgimiento tribal: The Pop Group y The Slits
notes.text: Dennis Bovell, el único productor británico a la altura de Lee Perry y King Tubby (sound system Jah Sufferer, Matumbi, lovers rock, el LP Strictly Dub Wize como Blackbeard, la música de Linton Kwesi Johnson), produce a The Pop Group y a The Slits. El milenarismo rasta («armagideon», Babylon) resuena entre los bohemios blancos como exiliados internos.

refs.q: y aprendían del reggae roots y del dub contemporáneos
refs.para: Más que los riffs rama-lama' o los acordes bluseros, el panteón postpunk de innovadores de la guitarra se mostró partidario de la angularidad, de un definido registro punzante. Evitaban los solos, excepto por breves irrupciones de la guitarra principal, que se integraba a partir de una forma de tocar predominantemente orientada hacia el ritmo. En lugar de un sonido "gordo", guitarristas como David Byrne, de Talking Heads, Martin Bramah, de The Fall, o Viv Albertine, de The Slits, preferían un estilo de "guitarra rítmica escuálida", inspirado con frecuencia en el reggae o el funk. Este estilo más compacto y descarnado de tocar la guitarra no pretendía llenar cada rincón del espacio sonoro, lo cual permitió que el bajo pasara al frente, abandonando su rol tradicionalmente insignificante, de apoyo, hasta transformarse en voz instrumental principal, que cumplía una función melódica incluso cuando se ocupaba de llevar el groove. En este sentido, los bajistas postpunk se ponían al día con las innovaciones de Sly Stone y James Brown, y aprendían del reggae roots y del dub contemporáneos. Al buscar un sonido militante y agresivamente monolítico, el punk en su mayor parte había purgado el elemento negro del rock, cortando los vínculos con el R&B y rechazando, al mismo tiempo, la música disco por escapista e insulsa. Hacia 1978, sin embargo, empezó a difundirse entre los círculos postpunk el concepto de una música dance peligrosa, expresada en términos de perverted disco y de avant funk.

refs.q: revolución puramente sonora, una psicodelia africanizada
refs.para: El periodista Jon Savage hizo la crítica de Bollocks para la revista Sounds y hoy recuerda haberlo sentido "como una lápida, sofocante, sin ningún espacio en la música", un comentario que ubica el fracaso del disco en su carencia de dub. En comparación con la producción del reggae -pura neblina de reverbs centelleantes, efectos desorientadores e intermitentes volutas ectoplasmáticas-, la gran mayoría de los discos de punk sonaban simplemente retrógrados, atascados a mediados de los monocromáticos sesenta en mono, varados en algún lugar anterior a la paleta tímbrica ampliada y la brujería estereofónica de la psicodelia. Las bandas más perspicaces de todas aquellas que venían originalmente del punk sabían que tenían mucho por hacer para ponerse al día. Algunas de ellas, como The Clash y The Ruts, tomaron principalmente el aspecto de protesta del roots reggae: las consignas lanzadas abiertamente y el sermoneo de "Get Up Stand Up" de los Wailers y el chic radical del personaje de guerrillero rasta de Peter Tosh. En el extremo opuesto, las bandas postpunk más aventureras reaccionaron al reggae como si este fuera una revolución puramente sonora, una psicodelia africanizada que metamorfoseaba los contornos y alteraba la percepción. Durante la media década que va de 1977 a 1981, fueron exactamente la producción espacializada y los ritmos sofisticados pero elementales del reggae los que sentaron la base para todas las bandas postpunk que buscaban experimentar.

refs.q: Lydon había entrado en contacto con la cultura de los sound systems gracias a su amigo Don Letts
refs.para: Coleccionista fanático de reggae desde hacía ya mucho tiempo, Lydon había entrado en contacto con la cultura de los sound systems gracias a su amigo Don Letts, un DJ negro que pasaba música en el legendario antro punk The Roxy, a menudo reconocido como el responsable de haber hecho que la audiencia punk l . Las house parties o rent parties [fiestas de casa o fiestas de alquiler] eran reuniones sociales que nacieron en el Harlem durante la década del veinte, en las que los inquilinos de un edificio solían contratar a un músico o a una banda para recaudar el dinero necesario para pagar el alquiler. Fueron cruciales en el desarrollo del jazz y el blues. Los sound systems [sistemas de sonido] surgieron en los ghettos de Kingsron, Jamaica, en la década del cincuenta, y eran fiestas que se hacían en la calle, musicalizadas por un DJ, ingenieros de sonido y MC que trabajaban juntos desde un camión o una camioneta itinerante, equipada con una potencia, un tocadiscos y parlantes. Fueron de vital importancia para el surgimiento de estilos musicales como el ska, el reggae, el rocksteady y el dub, y llegaron al Reino Unido junto con los inmigrantes jamaiquinos que se instalaron allí en la década del setenta. [N. de la T.]

refs.q: por ese entonces el único productor de reggae británico lo suficientemente brillante como para soportar la comparación
refs.para: Para grabar "She Is Beyond Good and Evil", The Pop Group se asoció con Dennis Bovell, por ese entonces el único productor de reggae británico lo suficientemente brillante como para soportar la comparación con los genios jamaiquinos como Lee Perry y King Tubby. Figura clave en la escena reggae del Reino Unido, Bovell había operado el sound system Jah Sufferer Hi Fi, había fundado la popular banda de roots reggae británica Matumbi y había sido uno de los pioneros de ese género inmensamente exitoso llama- do "lover's rock" (una fusión británica entre el reggae jamaiquino y el soul suave americano que las mujeres adoraban). Como si todo esto no fuera suficiente, Bovell también había compuesto y producido la música de acompañamiento para los discos del poeta y activista Linton Kwesi Johnson y había editado sus propios LP -Strictly Dub Wize, entre ellos- bajo el seudónimo de Blackbeard. El espectro musical de Bovell iba mucho más allá del reggae, sin embargo. Había sido el guitarrista líder de una banda a la The Jimi Hendrix Experience llamada Stonehenge y creía que había sido Jimi quien había creado el primer track dub de todos los tiempos cuando sacó, en 1 967, "Third Sto ne from the Sun".

similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El reggae se populariza en el Reino Unido con Prince Buster y Desmond Dekker; Jimmy Cliff lo casa con el «paz y amor» hippy y los Maytals le dan nombre. Los sound systems de los guetos convierten a los «selectors» en los verdaderos animadores: el «toasting» sobre los discos será tan importante como la música. Bob Marley y los Wailers lo llevan a Occidente; Burning Spear firma quizá su cima artística (Marcus Garvey). Los ingenieros remezclan las caras B quitando las voces: King Tubby inventa el dub usando la mesa de mezclas como un instrumento, y Lee Perry (Super Ape) y Augustus Pablo fijan el canon.

podcast.title: Birth Environment (c. 1968)
podcast.body: Reggae emerged around 1968 in Jamaica, born out of a tumultuous period that saw the disillusionment of post-independence celebrations, rampant poverty in Kingston exacerbated by government bulldozing of squatter communities, and systemic political corruption that failed to address citizens' urgent needs for jobs. "It was in that environment that reggae was born around 1968."

podcast.title: Momentum Building (1972)
podcast.body: Reggae began to gain notable momentum in 1972, a year that coincided with the release of the influential Jamaican film "The Harder They Come," which featured Jimmy Cliff's popular title track and helped bring the genre to a wider audience. "We can see a bit of reggae momentum building in 1972, the same year that the film The Harder They Come was released and Jimmy Cliff made the title track to that movie's soundtrack, a hit."

podcast.title: 1977 British Context
podcast.body: In 1977, reggae was not as ubiquitous as it is today; its growing popularity in Britain was spurred by the political and economic situation in Jamaica, which led many Jamaicans to immigrate to Britain under a soon-to-be-eliminated Commonwealth law. "Ari developed a taste for reggae. And this is more radical than it sounds right now. See today, reggae and scott, that's everywhere, right? Not so in 1977, but that was changing thanks to the political and economic situation in Jamaica."

podcast.title: Disco's Impact (1977)
podcast.body: The overwhelming dominance of disco in 1977, both in dance clubs and on radio, swept over the music industry "like a tidal wave" and significantly hampered reggae's ability to achieve mainstream success in the American market. "My theory on this is very simple disco disco was king not just on the dance floor, but on the radio in 1977 it came over the music industry like a title wave. And reggae did not stand much of a chance."

podcast.title: First "True" Reggae Hit (1980)
podcast.body: According to music historian Tim Breham, the first "true reggae hit single" to break through in the United States did not occur until 1980, exemplified by Blondie's successful cover of "The Tide Is High." "He argues that the first true reggae hit single in the United States did not come until 1980."

podcast.title: "Computer Reggae" Shift (1985)
podcast.body: The landscape of reggae on black radio began to transform around 1985 with the advent of "computer reggae," a subgenre that incorporated sounds more akin to hip hop, thereby making it more accessible and appealing to a broader black audience. "That began to change in 1985 with what he called computer reggae, which sounded more like hip hop."

podcast.title: Musical Exploration (2005)
podcast.body: Sinead O'Connor fully embraced the reggae genre with her 2005 release, *Throw Down Your Arms*, a double reggae album recorded in Jamaica with the renowned production duo Sly & Robbie. This album also provided an opportunity to record Bob Marley's "War." "In 2005, she released Throw Down Your Arms, a double reggae album recorded in Jamaica with the production crew of Slian Robby."

podcast.title: "Rock Enough" for Radio Issue
podcast.body: Despite strategic marketing efforts to portray Bob Marley as a rock star, reggae, and by extension Marley's music, was arguably not considered "rock enough" for mainstream radio in the 1970s, leading to more airplay for reggae-inspired rock rather than authentic reggae tracks. "I think that even though Bob Marley was marketed as a rock star, he and by default reggae was not rock enough for the radio."

podcast.title: Arrangement Limitations (70s)
podcast.body: Ken Williams observed in 1975 that reggae struggled to compete with mainstream 70s rock and pop due to its lack of "mugs and the strings," referring to the synthesizers and orchestral arrangements that were integral to the popular sound of those genres. "He said in 1975 that he did not think that reggae could compete with the mugs and the strings, meaning that reggae did not have the synthesizers and orchestral arrangements that were such an integral part of rock and pop in the 70s."

podcast.title: Authenticity Dilemma (70s)
podcast.body: The issue of authenticity significantly challenged reggae in the 1970s, much like it affected rock in the 1980s and folk music in the 1960s after Bob Dylan's shift to electric, as purists often dismissed popular manifestations of the genre as "watered down." "The question of authenticity plagued reggae in the 70s in a way it plagued rock in the 80s and maybe even the way it plagued folk music in the 60s, especially after Dylan went electric."

podcast.body: Reggae music is listed as one of the basic and enduring sounds that will never go away, but is continuously challenged by new genres. "The basic sounds are still with us. podcast.title: Black Radio Avoidance (70s)
podcast.body: During the 1970s, black radio stations in America generally avoided playing reggae, perceiving its sound as too "primitive" when compared to the more sophisticated and elaborately produced American rhythm and blues and disco music of the era. "Black radio stayed away from reggae because it sounded too primitive when compared to American rhythm and blues."

podcast.title: Bluebeat in Coventry
podcast.body: In the industrial city of Coventry, many Jamaican immigrants settled, bringing their music, which was then referred to as Bluebeat. This genre existed alongside Northern Soul, R&B, and other British youth music movements. "industrial city of Coventry... home to many Jamaican immigrants in their music, which was now being called Bluebeat. In Coventry, Bluebeat existed alongside several other genres, Northern Soul, R&B, Reggae, as well as some of the music of the British youth movements, the mods, the rockers, the Teddyboys, and of course, the punk rockers."

podcast.title: Cultural and Musical Mixing
podcast.body: Jamaican immigrants, seeking jobs in post-war labor-shortage Britain, became part of the British working class, leading to an inevitable mixing of cultures and, consequently, music, greatly influencing British artists like The Slits and The Clash. "See, the UK was still suffering a certain amount of post-war labor shortages, and these immigrants became part of the British working class, and that led to an inevitable mixing of cultures. podcast.title: Diverse Nature
podcast.body: Reggae is characterized as a multifaceted genre, comprising "many styles" and "many messages," emphasizing that attempts to narrowly classify it miss its true essence and its significant, complex place in the history of rock and pop music. "Reggae is not just one thing, it is many styles, it is many messages. To try to classify it as one thing is to miss the point, and to dismiss its place and rock and pop history is to have an incomplete history."

podcast.body: Researchers have found that dogs' stress levels significantly decrease when exposed to reggae music, a phenomenon that Scotland seems to lead studies in. podcast.body: Scientific studies indicate that dogs respond positively to certain types of music, particularly those with rhythms close to their own heartbeat, to help with issues like separation anxiety, hyperactivity, or fear of thunderstorms. podcast.title: Early Distribution and Censorship
podcast.body: In its formative years, reggae music was primarily consumed at dances because many Jamaicans could not afford to buy records, and the Jamaican government frequently banned much of the genre from airwaves due to its overtly political and critical lyrical content. "Many Jamaicans could not afford records, and the Jamaican government would not let a lot of reggae on the air because it was too political."

podcast.body: Reggae, along with ska, was incorporated into the vision of punk rock by bands in the mid-1990s, reminiscent of how early punk bands like The Slits channeled their sound through reggae. podcast.body: Massive Attack extensively drew from Jamaican reggae music, deconstructing it and slowing down its often fast or simple bases to extremely slow tempos. podcast.title: Introduced to Punks by Don Letts
podcast.body: In the 1970s, Don Letts, a DJ, played a crucial role in introducing reggae music to a new generation of punk kids in clubs. With few punk records available at the time, Jamaican music, including reggae, served as the initial soundtrack for the burgeoning punk scene. "He was the DJ who introduced reggae and dub to a new generation of these punk kids in the 1970s in clubs where they hung out. See, there were no punk records yet, so that music, Jamaican music, dub music, black music became theirs until they had some punk records to listen to."

podcast.title: Musical Ancestry
podcast.body: Reggae is characterized as a synthesis of various musical styles, drawing heavily from Jamaican Mento (local folk/country music), dancehall swing (like Benny Goodman or Glenn Miller), and a significant infusion of American rhythm and blues or early rock (such as Fats Domino), with powerful radio signals from Miami reaching Kingston playing a key role in its development. "It is the product of a lot of different musical styles, much of it from the United States, not along by some powerful radio stations out of Miami, whose signals reached Kingston."

podcast.title: Normalization in White Rock
podcast.body: Elvis Costello made the connection between reggae and white rock even more overt with his song "Watching the Detectives," which helped normalize reggae rhythms in white rock music. This normalization made reggae more commercially acceptable for a mass audience than hardcore punk and enabled other bands, most notably The Police, to achieve chart success by adopting the approach. "Once reggae was normalized in white rock by Costello, on a song that helped break him in America and was also a number 15 hit in his UK homeland, other bands were able to take the approach and run up the charts with it."
